extracted.intended_audience: labor law practitioners, employers, unions, NLRB practitioners, and regulated parties affected by joint-employer determinations
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for determining when two entities are joint employers of the same employees under the National Labor Relations Act, as discussed in the NLRB final rule, the 2020 rule, and related court guidance. Covers threshold common-law employment, what counts as 'essential terms and conditions of employment,' and the forms/extent of control that trigger bargaining obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold common-law employment relationship (§103.40(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party seeking to demonstrate joint-employer status must make an initial showing that the putative joint employer has a common-law employment relationship with particular employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent evidence that an entity is the common-law employer of particular employees, there is no basis for a joint-employer finding under the final rule. This threshold excludes entities whose relationship to the performance of the work is too attenuated to support a common-law employment finding (e.g., merely setting hours of operation without other indicia of common-law control).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustive list of essential terms and conditions (2020 Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2020 Rule defined a closed set of 'essential terms and conditions of employment': wages, benefits, hours of work, hiring, discharge, discipline, supervision, and direction. (29 CFR 103.40(b))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The closed list was adopted to ensure any required bargaining would be meaningful and to provide predictability; the 2020 Rule also provided term-specific guidance (see hiring, supervision examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of workplace health and safety as an essential term (final rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule treats workplace health and safety as an essential term or condition of employment such that an entity that possesses or exercises control over workplace health and safety may be a joint employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An entity that solely memorializes compliance with legal obligations pertaining to health and safety will not for that reason alone be regarded as a joint employer; but entities that exercise discretion over particular employees' workplace health and safety are properly treated as joint employers because bargaining with all entities that exercise such control is central to collective rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession and exercise of substantial direct and immediate control (2020 Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the 2020 Rule, an entity may be a joint employer only if it possesses and exercises 'such substantial direct and immediate control over one or more essential terms or conditions of [employees'] employment as would warrant finding that the entity meaningfully affects matters relating to the employment relationship with those employees.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation requires active and substantial involvement (e.g., hiring, supervising, setting wages/hours, disciplining). It was intended to impose a substantiality requirement and provide a 'discernible and predictable' standard to guide regulated parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'substantial direct and immediate control'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Substantial direct and immediate control' means direct and immediate control that has a regular or continuous consequential effect on an essential term or condition of employment; control exercised only on a sporadic, isolated, or de minimis basis is not 'substantial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a scope/extent test: look for regular/continuous consequential effects. Sporadic or merely occasional influence should not satisfy the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiring: what counts as exercising direct and immediate control (2020 examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: An entity exercises direct and immediate control over hiring if it actually determines which particular employees will be hired and which employees will not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An entity does not exercise direct and immediate control over hiring by requesting changes in staffing levels or by setting minimal hiring standards such as those required by government regulation. The example draws a line between decision-making over individual hires versus general staffing requests or minimal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision: what counts as exercising direct and immediate control (2020 examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: An entity exercises direct and immediate control over supervision by actually instructing another employer's employees how to perform their work or by actually issuing employee performance appraisals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing instructions that are limited and routine and that consist primarily of telling employees what work to perform, or where and when to perform it, but not how to perform it, does not constitute direct and immediate supervision for joint-employer purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect control, contractually reserved authority, and other forms of control (2020 treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2020 Rule treated indirect control, contractually reserved but never exercised authority, and control over mandatory bargaining subjects other than essential terms as probative of joint-employer status only to the extent they supplement and reinforce evidence of possession or exercise of direct and immediate control over a particular essential term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the 2020 Rule these other forms of control could not, standing alone, establish joint-employer status; they serve to supplement direct-control evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control exercised through an intermediary remains direct and immediate
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct and immediate control exercised through an intermediary remains direct and immediate for joint-employer analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The common law does not permit use of intermediaries or controlled third parties to avoid creation of a master-servant relationship; where an entity exercises actual control through an intermediary, that control is treated as direct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final rule: mere possession of authority to control is dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule provides that to 'share or codetermine' means for an employer to possess the authority to control (whether directly, indirectly, or both), or to exercise the power to control (whether directly, indirectly, or both), one or more of the employees' essential terms and conditions of employment — making mere possession of such authority sufficient to establish joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This removes the need for proof of actual exercise, much less substantial exercise, and treats unexercised contractual reservations or indirect forms of control as independently sufficient. Under this approach a putative joint-employer may be found based on the mere existence of a reserved contractual right or indirect authority to affect an essential term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independently sufficient role of indirect control and reserved rights (final rule change)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule makes contractually reserved but unexercised control and indirect control not merely probative but independently sufficient to establish joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this change, indirect control (including control via intermediaries and other non-direct mechanisms) and reserved contractual authority can alone trigger joint-employer obligations without being tied to evidence of actual direct control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional approach to assessing 'work rules or directions'
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguous language in employee handbooks or 'work rules or directions' is to be assessed using a functional approach to determine whether the putative joint employer possesses or exercises the requisite control over essential terms and conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will take a functional approach, focusing on how the rule operates in practice rather than on formalistic labels; ambiguous or broad handbook language does not automatically convert an entity into a joint employer without functional evidence of control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicially defined outer limits: common-law boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The common law sets the outer limits of a permissible joint-employer standard under the Act; the Board's rulemaking must 'color within the common-law lines' identified by the judiciary, though the Board may adopt a narrower standard to promote the Act's policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking must be informed by common-law agency doctrine and court guidance; the Board cannot adopt a standard more expansive than common law permits even if it believes policy favors doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-step inquiry — 'meaningful collective bargaining' and 'extent' of control (D.C. Circuit critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: The D.C. Circuit required the Board to delineate what terms are 'essential' and to clarify when a putative joint employer's control over essential terms is sufficient to permit 'meaningful collective bargaining' — i.e., to consider the extent, form, frequency, and exercise of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have criticized standards that are 'inclusive' or 'non-exhaustive' regarding essential terms and have demanded clarity on what 'meaningful' bargaining requires; extent (how substantial the control is) has been a central focus of this critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-specific context and uniform application
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board applies a uniform joint-employer standard to all entities within its jurisdiction but will be sensitive to industry-specific norms and practices when considering whether an entity is a joint employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board declined requests to exempt particular industries (construction, franchises, staffing, healthcare) but will consider relevant industry context as part of the factual assessment of whether control exists and what its effects are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy rationale for limiting joint-employer obligations (2020 Rule policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2020 Rule's policy rationale: impose bargaining obligations only on entities that actually control essential working conditions to avoid subjecting innocent parties to liability and to provide certainty and predictable lines for regulated parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A less demanding, fuzzier standard could subject arm's-length contracting parties to liability for others' unfair labor practices and complicate distinguishing such parties from genuine joint employers; preserving the element of direct and immediate control was intended to provide 'certainty beforehand.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing routine contracting parameters from indirect control (D.C. Circuit point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence showing routine parameters of contracting (e.g., controlling basic contours of a contracted-for service) should not be given weight as indirect control that bears on workers' essential terms; courts require distinguishing such routine contracting from indirect control that truly affects essential employment terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of inappropriate weight include counting a firm's specification of the number of workers or composition of a contracted service as proof of joint-employer indirect control; the analysis should focus on whether the indirect mechanism actually affects essential terms of employment.
